content: Building a new ESPHome sensor node for the garage — I want temperature, humidity, and a PIR motion sensor all on one ESP32 board. The garage isn't heated so it needs to handle temperature swings from -10°F to 110°F.
The ESP32 itself handles that range fine. For temperature and humidity, a BME280 would be a good choice — it's accurate and handles the full range. For the PIR, an AM312 is compact and low power.

Yeah, the BME280 is what I use everywhere else. I want to add a door contact sensor too — magnetic reed switch on the garage door so I can track open/close state. The ESPHome binary sensor platform handles that natively.

A reed switch is the simplest approach. Wire it between a GPIO pin and ground, enable the internal pull-up in ESPHome, and you have a reliable open/close sensor. You could also add a template sensor that tracks how long the door has been open.

Good idea on the duration tracker — I want an automation that alerts me if the garage door is open for more than 30 minutes. I'll use a Home Assistant automation for that since the logic spans multiple sensors. The ESPHome node just publishes state, the orchestration layer handles the business logic.

Clean separation of concerns. The sensor node is responsible for data collection and publishing, Home Assistant handles the automation logic. Same as keeping your microservices focused on one responsibility.

That's literally how I think about it. Each ESPHome node is a microservice — single responsibility, well-defined interface (MQTT topics), independently deployable. The thing is, I actually use the same CI/CD mindset for firmware updates — OTA updates pushed from a central repo.
